_comment: Council terms in one place: the public page /how-council-works renders it, the web app's timeline stage lines come from each term's `stages`, and the AI clients turn `in_the_record` (how Langford's minutes phrase it) and `we_write` (the plain words this site uses) into prompt blocks (apps/web/app/services/ai/glossary-prompt.ts, pipeline/ai/glossary.py). Public text follows docs/writing-style.md. Bump version when a `we_write` or `stages` line changes so stages that write summaries can be rerun with --stale. A term's `match` is a case-insensitive regex for the word forms pages show; the first match on a page gets a dashed underline, a hover definition and a link (components/term.tsx).

groups.title: Kinds of meetings
groups.intro: Langford Council meets in public, usually twice a month. Different kinds of meetings are allowed to do different things, and the name tells you which.

terms.means: Council's scheduled meeting, usually on the first and third Monday of the month. This is where most decisions happen. Anyone can attend, and the video is online.
terms.in_the_record: "Council Meeting", "Council Minutes".

terms.means: A meeting called outside the regular schedule, with at least a day's notice. Langford holds quite a few, often in the afternoon before a regular meeting, usually for one or two items.
terms.in_the_record: "Special Council Meeting", "SP Council Minutes".

terms.means: All of Council sitting as a committee so they can talk things through less formally. It can only recommend; the actual decision comes at a later Council meeting.
terms.in_the_record: "Committee of the Whole", "COTW". Its motions read "THAT Committee of the Whole recommend that Council…". Langford uses it mainly for budget sessions.
terms.we_write: We say "the committee recommended", never "approved". A committee's vote isn't the decision.

terms.means: A group of resident volunteers and staff that advises Council on one area. Langford has a Sustainable Development Advisory Committee and a Community Advisory Committee, plus a Board of Variance that decides small zoning exceptions on its own. Committees recommend, and Council decides.
terms.in_the_record: "Sustainable Development Advisory Committee", "Community Advisory Committee". Their advice reaches Council as "Committee Resolutions" or "Community Advisory Committee Meeting Resolutions – <date>".
terms.we_write: We say a committee "recommended" something, and name the committee only when it matters to the story.

terms.means: A meeting where residents can speak or write to Council about a proposed zoning or community plan change before Council decides. It happens after first reading and before third reading, and once it closes Council can't take any more input on that proposal. Since 2023, provincial law doesn't allow a hearing for housing that already fits the community plan, and Council can waive one in other cases, so many rezonings now go ahead without one.
terms.in_the_record: "PUBLIC HEARING", usually called to order just before the Council meeting the same evening, with "PUBLIC INPUT" then "Mayor closed the Public Hearing at 7:19 pm". When none is held: "Notice of Public Hearing Being Waived".
terms.we_write: We say "residents could speak or write to Council about…", and give how many spoke and what they said when the record has it. When no hearing was held, we say so rather than leaving you to assume there was one.

stages.public_hearing: Residents could speak or write to council about the proposal.

terms.means: The part of a meeting the public can't attend. Provincial law lists the only reasons allowed, such as buying or selling land, legal advice, labour talks or personnel matters. Council has to say which reason applies, and anything decided behind closed doors is reported afterwards.
terms.in_the_record: "THAT Council close the meeting to the public pursuant to section 90 (1) (e) of the Community Charter to consider…", "In-camera", then "RISE AND REPORT" when it reopens.
terms.we_write: We say "closed meeting" and give the reason in plain words ("about buying land"), not the section number.

terms.means: When a closed meeting ends, Council comes back into open session and reports any decisions it's allowed to make public.
terms.in_the_record: "RISE AND REPORT" as an agenda heading after the closed part.
terms.we_write: We say "after the closed meeting, Council reported that…".

terms.means: Routine items bundled together and passed in one vote without discussion. Any member can pull an item out to talk about it on its own.
terms.we_write: We leave consent-agenda housekeeping out of summaries unless an item was pulled out and debated.
terms.in_the_record: "CONSENT AGENDA", "THAT Council adopt the recommendations for each item of the Consent Agenda as presented", with "(RECEIVE)" or "(ADOPT)" per item.

terms.means: Time set aside for residents to speak to Council. A delegation books ahead in writing and gets five minutes on any subject. Public participation is open to anyone in the room, three minutes each, on items that are on that night's agenda. Council can't hear new input on a proposal that has already had its public hearing.
terms.in_the_record: "DELEGATIONS", "PUBLIC PARTICIPATION". Speakers are logged as "M. Wignall, Langford Resident – re: item 5.1 – The speaker expressed support for…".
terms.we_write: We say someone "spoke to Council" or "asked Council to…", and name speakers only the way the minutes name them.

terms.means: The agenda is the plan for a meeting, published a couple of days ahead. The minutes are the official written record of what was decided, approved at a later meeting. Minutes record decisions and votes, not everything that was said. For that, there's the video.
terms.we_write: Something on the agenda isn't a decision yet. We say what happened, not what was listed.

groups.title: How Council decides
groups.intro: Everything Council decides starts as a motion that members vote on. The minutes record the wording of each motion and how the vote went.

terms.means: A proposal that Council votes on. One member moves it and another seconds it before anyone can discuss it. Every decision starts this way.
terms.in_the_record: "MOVED BY: MORLEY", "SECONDED: WAGNER", then "THAT Council…". Surnames only, no titles.
terms.we_write: We call it a "decision" once it has been voted on and a "proposal" before that. We don't put "motion" in a headline.

terms.means: A decision Council makes with a single vote, with no bylaw involved. Most of what Council does, like awarding contracts, giving grants and asking staff to do things, is done by resolution.
terms.we_write: We say "Council decided", "approved" or "asked staff to".

terms.means: The motion passed. When nobody is listed as opposed, everyone in the room voted yes.
terms.in_the_record: "Motion CARRIED." Recent minutes don't write "carried unanimously"; a passed motion with no "OPPOSED:" line was unanimous.
terms.we_write: We say "passed" or "approved", and give the count when the vote was split: "passed 6–1".

terms.means: The motion failed.
terms.in_the_record: "Motion DEFEATED."
terms.we_write: We say "rejected" or "voted down".

terms.means: The minutes name only the members who voted against, right after the result. When nobody is named, everyone present voted yes. A member who stays silent counts as a yes, and a tie means the motion is defeated. Because the minutes don't list the yes votes, the vote counts on this site come from who attended and who was named as opposed.
terms.in_the_record: "OPPOSED: Councillors Guiry, Szpak, Yacucha, and Harder." or "OPPOSED: Mayor Goodmanson" under the result line. Older minutes: "(Voting against: …)".
terms.we_write: We say "passed 5–2, with X and Y opposed". We never guess who voted yes.

terms.means: A change to a motion before the vote. Council votes on the amendment first, then on the motion as changed.
terms.we_write: We say what the change did ("cut the fee to $200"), not "the amendment carried".
terms.in_the_record: "Amendment on the Main Motion:", its own moved, seconded and result lines, then "On the Main Motion as amended:".

terms.means: Sent to staff or a committee for more work before Council decides.
terms.in_the_record: "THAT Council refer this item to staff…".
terms.we_write: We say "sent back to staff" or "asked staff to report back".

terms.means: In Langford's minutes, to "table" an item means to put it off, often to a named later meeting. It's rare, a few times a year at most, but it still happens. In much of Canada "tabled" means the opposite, to present something, so the word reads both ways and this site avoids it.
terms.in_the_record: "THAT Council table this item to the Special Council Meeting on May 9, 2024", "THAT the main motion be tabled". About a dozen motions since 2009, the latest in 2026. Residents speaking at hearings say "table" too.
terms.we_write: We say "postponed to May 9", or "set aside" when no date was given, and "presented" for something brought before Council. Never "tabled".

terms.means: A member lets Council know they'll bring a motion to a future meeting. Nothing is decided yet.
terms.we_write: We say a member "gave notice that they will propose…". It isn't counted as a decision.
terms.in_the_record: "Councillor Harder introduced the following Notice of Motion:", then moved at the next regular meeting under "NOTICE OF MOTION".

terms.means: Council cancels something it decided earlier. The record rarely says why.
terms.in_the_record: "THAT Council rescind first, second and third readings of Bylaw No. 2121…", or an agenda label like "(RESCIND FIRST THREE READINGS AND GIVE NEW FIRST THREE READINGS AS AMENDED)".
terms.we_write: We say Council "cancelled its earlier decision to…" and don't guess at the reason.

stages.rescinded_reading: Council cancelled an earlier reading of the bylaw.
stages.rescinded_adoption: Council cancelled the bylaw's adoption and its readings.

terms.means: The mover took the motion back before a vote, or nobody seconded it, so it was never voted on.
terms.in_the_record: "The motion was withdrawn.", "received permission of the seconder and withdrew the motion", "The motion died on the floor for want of a seconder."
terms.we_write: We say the member "withdrew the proposal". There was no vote, so there's no count.

terms.means: A written report from City staff that explains an issue and recommends what Council should do. Council often adopts the recommendation word for word.
terms.we_write: We say "staff recommended…". The report is usually the best source for what a decision actually does.

terms.means: A member who could personally gain from a decision has to say so and leave the room. They don't take part in the vote.
terms.in_the_record: "Councillor Harder declared a perceived conflict of interest … and left the meeting at 9:51 pm".
terms.we_write: We say the member "left the room for the vote".

terms.means: Recommendations from an advisory committee, brought to Council in a batch. Council votes on whether to act on them.
terms.in_the_record: "COMMITTEE RESOLUTIONS", "Community Advisory Committee Meeting Resolutions – January 27, 2026".
terms.we_write: We say "on the committee's advice, Council…".

groups.title: How a bylaw becomes law
groups.intro: A bylaw is a city law. Council votes on it several times before it takes effect, and each of those votes is called a reading. This site explains each step in plain words instead of naming it.

terms.means: A city law. Zoning, fees, noise rules, parking and the budget are all bylaws. Each one has a number and goes through readings before it's adopted.
terms.in_the_record: "BYLAW NO. 2220", with a long formal title such as "City of Langford Housing Agreement (777 Station Avenue) Bylaw No. 2220, 2025".
terms.we_write: We say what the bylaw does and keep its number out of headlines and summaries: "new garbage fees", not "Bylaw 2284".

terms.means: Council votes on a bylaw several times, and each vote is called a reading. BC bylaws need three readings and then adoption. Langford usually gives all three readings at one meeting. Provincial law then requires at least a day before adoption, so most bylaws are adopted at a later meeting.
terms.in_the_record: Agenda labels: "(FIRST, SECOND AND THIRD READINGS)", "(SECOND AND THIRD READINGS)", "(FIRST READING)", "(ADOPTION)".
terms.we_write: We explain the step instead of naming it: "introduced", "one step from final approval", "made final".

terms.means: The bylaw is introduced and Council agrees to consider it. On its own, first reading is mostly used for community plan changes; most bylaws get all three readings at once.
terms.we_write: We say "introduced" or "took the first step toward…".

stages.first: Introduced to council. A bylaw needs several readings before it becomes law.

terms.means: Council approves the bylaw in principle. It's usually given together with first and third reading in a single vote.
terms.we_write: We say "approved in principle".

stages.second: Council approved the bylaw's content in principle.

terms.means: Council approves the final wording. Only adoption is left, usually at a later meeting (the same night for zoning and community plan bylaws). Most of the debate has happened by this point, so a bylaw that passes third reading almost always goes on to be adopted.
terms.we_write: We say "one step from final approval". We don't add "a later vote is still needed", because the phrase already says that.

stages.third: Council approved the final wording. Adoption is the last step.
stages.second_third: Council approved the content and final wording. Adoption is the last step.

terms.means: The last vote, after which the bylaw is law and there's nothing more for Council to decide. In the minutes, "adopted" always means this final step. Although a bylaw that has passed third reading has effectively been agreed, it isn't law until this vote, and sometimes a project changes or stalls in between. Most bylaws have to wait at least a day after third reading; zoning and community plan bylaws are the exception and can be adopted the same night.
terms.in_the_record: "(ADOPTION)", "That Bylaw No. 2284 be adopted".
terms.we_write: We say "made final" or "final approval". On this site a bylaw is shown as adopted only after this vote: a topic gets its "Adopted" badge here, and a bylaw past third reading is "one step from final approval" until then. Each vote is counted on its own in a councillor's record, so voting for the readings and then for adoption shows as two votes. We don't call a plain resolution "adopted"; that's "passed".

groups.title: Land and building
groups.intro: Most of what Council decides is about land: what can be built where, and on what conditions.

terms.means: Changing what a property may be used for, or how big a building there can be. It needs a bylaw with readings and adoption, usually comes with conditions, and sometimes has a public hearing.
terms.in_the_record: "Langford Zoning Bylaw, Amendment No. 740 (2609 Sooke Road), Bylaw No. 2211, 2026"; file numbers like "Z25-0008".
terms.we_write: We say "rezoning of 2609 Sooke Road for 47 homes" and keep file numbers out.

terms.means: Langford's long-term plan for where homes, shops and parks should go. A project that doesn't fit needs a plan amendment, which is itself a bylaw.
terms.in_the_record: "OCP", "Official Community Plan Amendment".
terms.we_write: We say "community plan", spelled out, never "OCP".

terms.means: Approval of how a building will look and sit on its lot, in the areas the community plan covers. It isn't a zoning change.
terms.in_the_record: "DP", "Development Permit".
terms.we_write: We say Council "approved the design of…", never "DP".

terms.means: Permission to break one specific zoning rule, such as a setback or a height limit, for one property. Neighbours get notice, and Council decides.
terms.in_the_record: "DVP24-0012", "varied pursuant to section 498". Decided under the agenda heading "NOTICE OF INTENT" after neighbours are notified; small variances can be decided by staff or the Board of Variance.
terms.we_write: We say "variance", or spell out what was allowed ("a taller building than the rules permit"). Never "DVP".

terms.means: The agenda heading under which Council decides variance and temporary use permits. Neighbours are notified first and can write or speak before the vote.
terms.in_the_record: "NOTICE OF INTENT", then the permit number.
terms.we_write: We name the permit and the property, not the heading.

terms.means: Permission to use a property for something its zoning doesn't allow, for up to three years. It can be renewed once.
terms.in_the_record: "TUP21-0006", "renewed … for a period of three years". Decided under "NOTICE OF INTENT".
terms.we_write: We say "temporary permit", never "TUP".

terms.means: A contract between the City and a developer that sets rents or who can live in certain homes, usually in exchange for a rezoning. It's adopted as a bylaw, so it goes through readings and adoption.
terms.we_write: We say "a deal to keep rents at…", with the numbers.
terms.in_the_record: "Housing Agreement (777 Station Avenue) Bylaw No. 2220".

terms.means: A promise registered on a property's title that binds future owners too, such as keeping a tree or building a path.
terms.in_the_record: "Section 219 covenant".
terms.we_write: We say "a condition on the land" and leave out "section 219".

terms.means: Fees developers pay toward the roads, parks, water and sewer that new growth needs.
terms.in_the_record: "DCC", "Development Cost Charge Bylaw".
terms.we_write: We say "developer fees for parks and roads", never "DCC".

terms.means: A set fee developers pay for each new home or lot, toward amenities like parks, recreation and daycare. Langford set it by bylaw in June 2026. Before that, contributions were negotiated deal by deal, in exchange for extra density.
terms.in_the_record: "Amenity Cost Charge Bylaw No. 2275". Older minutes: "contribution … as a bonus for increased density … towards the General Amenity Reserve Fund".
terms.we_write: We say "the developer will pay $X toward parks and recreation". For the older deals, "in exchange for extra density".

terms.means: Dividing one lot into several. Staff decide most of these; Council sees one when a bylaw or a road is involved.
terms.we_write: We say "split into three lots".

terms.means: Langford's five-year budget, adopted each spring as a bylaw before the tax rates are set. The first year of it is this year's budget.
terms.in_the_record: "2026–2030 Financial Plan Bylaw No. 2281".
terms.we_write: We say "the 2026 budget".

terms.means: Sets this year's property tax rates. It's adopted with the budget, by May 15.
terms.we_write: We say "property taxes", with the change for a typical home when the record gives it.
terms.in_the_record: "Tax Rates Bylaw No. 2282, 2026".

terms.means: A flat charge on every property in an area for one service, such as sewer, on top of regular property tax.
terms.we_write: We say "a $X-a-year charge on homes in…".

terms.means: Chairs Council meetings and has one vote, the same as everyone else. Elected city-wide every four years.
terms.we_write: We say "Mayor" with their name as the record gives it, and never guess pronouns.

terms.means: One of the six elected members besides the mayor. Each has one vote.
terms.we_write: We say "Councillor" with their name. We don't assume someone's title; we check the roster for the meeting date.

terms.means: City employees, led by the Chief Administrative Officer. They write the reports, make recommendations and carry out what Council decides. They don't vote.
terms.in_the_record: "Director of Community Planning & Climate Change", "Director of Development Services", "Corporate Officer", "CAO".
terms.we_write: We say "staff", or describe the role in plain words ("the City's planning director").

terms.means: Whoever is running the meeting. Usually that's the mayor; when the mayor is away, an acting mayor takes over on a rotation set each year.
A panel of appointed residents, separate from Council, that can allow small exceptions to zoning rules where following them would cause real hardship.
terms.we_write: We say "the Board of Variance allowed…", never "Council".
